title: English to First-Order Logic: the Sentence Templates
quickIdea: Every GATE translation question is one of a handful of sentence shapes. The rule that decides all of them: implication inside a universal, conjunction inside an existential.
remember: All A's are B's: for all x (A(x) implies B(x)).
Some A is B: there exists x (A(x) and B(x)).
No A's are B's: for all x (A(x) implies not B(x)), equivalently not (there exists x (A(x) and B(x))).
Some A's are not B's: there exists x (A(x) and not B(x)). This is exactly the negation of 'all A's are B's'.
Only A's are B's: for all x (not A(x) implies not B(x)), which by contraposition is the same as for all x (B(x) implies A(x)).
All and only A's are B's: for all x (A(x) if and only if B(x)) - both directions are needed.
Not all A's are B's: there exists x (A(x) and not B(x)).
The quantifier ranges over the whole domain, so the noun condition is written inside it: implication for the universal, conjunction for the existential.
More than one formula can be correct. 'Some boy is taller than all the girls' can put the universal inside or outside the existential.

example.prompt: Domain: the class. boy(x), girl(x), taller(x, y). Translate: some boys are taller than all the girls.
example.work: Outer quantifier is existential with a conjunction, because at least one boy must exist. Inside, the girls are described with a universal and an implication, because not everyone in the domain is a girl.
example.answer: There exists x (boy(x) and for all y (girl(y) implies taller(x, y))).

gateAngle: GATE CS 2004 Q.23 is this sentence, and the four options differ only in where the arrow and the and sit. GATE CS 2026 Set 2 Q.1 asks the same skill with a 'knows' relation, where the quantifier order also has to be right.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: See GATE CS 2004 Q.23 and GATE CS 2026 Set 2 Q.1 under this card's linked PYQs: both are translation questions where the wrong options differ only in the connective.
variations.why: In both, the existential carries a conjunction (the witness must be a boy, or a person) and the universal carries an implication.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Translate 'only students may enter the library', with S(x): x is a student and E(x): x may enter the library.
variations.answer: For all x (not S(x) implies not E(x)), equivalently for all x (E(x) implies S(x)).
variations.why: 'Only A's are B's' is the reverse implication, not the forward one. Reading it as for all x (S(x) implies E(x)) would say every student enters, which the sentence does not claim.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Translate 'some students did not submit every assignment'.
variations.answer: There exists x (student(x) and there exists y (assignment(y) and not submitted(x, y))).
variations.why: 'Did not submit every' is the negation of a universal, so it becomes an existential over a failing case; the outer 'some students' keeps its conjunction.

trap.what: Using the arrow with the existential, or the and with the universal.
trap.why: For all x (A(x) and B(x)) claims everything in the domain is an A, which is far stronger than 'all A's are B's'. There exists x (A(x) implies B(x)) is true as soon as one element is not an A, so it does not assert that any A exists.
trap.counterexample: Domain {1}, with A empty and B empty. 'All A's are B's' is vacuously true and is written with an implication; for all x (A(x) and B(x)) is false. And there exists x (A(x) implies B(x)) is true here, although 'some A is B' is false.

check.question: Translate 'no student failed' with S(x) and F(x).
check.answer: For all x (S(x) implies not F(x)), equivalently not (there exists x (S(x) and F(x))).
check.explanation: 'No A's are B's' is a universal with a negated consequent; the two forms are equivalent by the quantifier De Morgan law.
